passage:
At fifteen, Afreen's friend Asif kept imitating her way of saying "tomato" in front of the group, and it drew laughs every time. Afreen put her bag down and said in a calm voice, "I don't like that, and I'd like it to stop." No laughing, no shrugging it off. Asif blinked, then said, "Got it, sorry." He changed the subject to the match on Saturday, and after that he never did the voice again.

Nine years later, Afreen was at a team lunch and joked about her colleague Kunal's habit of losing his pen. Kunal smiled thinly and looked at his plate. Afreen noticed. Afterwards she found him at the coffee machine and said, "I'm sorry, that joke was not okay. I made it about you in front of everyone. I won't do it again." She did not add that he was too sensitive. Kunal nodded and said, "Thanks. I appreciate that." The next morning he stopped by her desk and shared a biscuit.

qa.q: What did Afreen say when Asif imitated her way of saying tomato?
qa.a: Afreen said, "I don't like that, and I'd like it to stop."

qa.q: How are Afreen's stances at fifteen and twenty-four connected?
qa.a: At fifteen Afreen says stop once, calmly, and Asif changes the subject; at twenty-four she tells Kunal she is sorry, without saying he was too sensitive. First she sets a boundary, and later she repairs trust after her own joke.

qa.q: What was Kunal probably feeling when he smiled thinly at the lunch joke?
qa.a: Kunal was embarrassed and a little hurt at being teased in front of everyone, though he hid it.
She named what was not okay and promised not to repeat it, without adding that Kunal was too sensitive, so the apology repaired trust instead of defending her intent.

grounding: Teasing and banter boundaries at two ages: a teenager saying stop calmly and being heard, and the same person later apologising cleanly for a hurtful joke.
